title: Reporting Hazards, Near Misses & Incidents
summary: Learn why safety reporting matters and how to communicate observations, uncertainty, near misses, and incidents accurately without exaggeration or unsupported conclusions.
objectives: Explain the difference between a hazard, near miss, and incident.
Identify the information that belongs in a useful safety report.
Distinguish facts, uncertainty, and assumptions when reporting.

vocab.def: An event that did not cause injury or damage but could have under slightly different circumstances.
An event or occurrence that may involve injury, damage, disruption, or another safety concern.
Communicating required information through the workplace's designated process.
A written or recorded account of observations, actions, decisions, or results.

sections.heading: Reporting helps organizations learn
sections.body: Safety reports can help a workplace identify recurring problems, changing conditions, training needs, and opportunities to prevent future harm.

sections.heading: Near misses matter
sections.body: A near miss may reveal a serious weakness even though nobody was hurt. Ignoring near misses can allow the same condition to produce a more serious outcome later.

sections.heading: Report facts accurately
sections.body: A useful report identifies what happened, when and where it happened, what was observed, what actions were taken, and what remains uncertain.

sections.heading: Do not invent conclusions
sections.body: Workers should not claim causes, blame, injuries, or technical findings they cannot support. Record facts and route technical or investigative conclusions to the appropriate authority.

practice.prompt: An object almost falls near a worker but nobody is injured. Why might this still need to be reported?
practice.answer: It may be a near miss that reveals a condition capable of causing harm in the future.

practice.prompt: You know what you observed but do not know what caused it. What should your report say?
practice.answer: Report the observed facts and clearly identify that the cause is unknown or unverified.

quiz.question: What makes a safety report useful?
options: Accurate facts, relevant context, actions taken, and clearly stated uncertainty
A confident guess about the cause
Removing details that could make the situation look serious
quiz.answer: Accurate facts, relevant context, actions taken, and clearly stated uncertainty

lab.objective: Write a simulated safety report that separates direct observations, actions taken, unresolved questions, and information requiring qualified review.
